chunks: "Doping is deliberately adding a very small, controlled amount of impurity atoms into a semiconductor to change how many free carriers it has and what type they are.
Pure silicon at room temperature has only about 10 to the 10 free carriers per cm³, out of 5 times 10 to the 22 atoms, so it conducts badly.
If I add phosphorus, which has five valence electrons, each atom donates an extra free electron and I get N-type.
If I add boron, with three valence electrons, each atom creates a hole and I get P-type. The amounts are tiny.
One dopant atom per million silicon atoms, one part per million, already increases the carrier density by a factor of about five million over intrinsic.
You can dial the doping from about 10 to the 14 to 10 to the 20 per cm³, which takes the resistivity from about 50 ohm-centimetres down to under a milli-ohm-centimetre.

In practice, we put the dopants in with ion implantation, where you fire ionized dopant atoms into the wafer, or with diffusion from a gas or solid source, then anneal to repair the damage and activate them.
That's how you make N and P regions to form diodes, transistors and resistors."
